title: The Minsk ATETS
subtitle: The reactors were buildable. After Chernobyl, nobody would live beside them.
summary: The Soviet Union began building a 2,000 MW dual-purpose nuclear plant 40 kilometres southeast of Minsk in 1983, with a purpose-built atomic town at Druzhny laid out on a butterfly plan and later housing about 1,200 evacuated Pripyat families. A Central Committee resolution of 1 July 1987 abandoned the plant after Chernobyl, the western wing of Druzhny was never built, and the site was completed instead as the fossil-fuelled Minsk CHPP-5, whose first unit ran in 1999.
lesson: Public tolerance is a project input like steel or capital; when it collapses, a technically sound plan becomes unbuildable overnight.
locationRole: Reactor site and its atomic town

title: Belene Nuclear Power Plant
subtitle: Two reactors bought, paid for and stored. Neither was ever installed.
summary: Bulgaria approved the Belene site in March 1981 and by the 1991 suspension had completed roughly 40 percent of Unit 1 site work and procured 80 percent of the major equipment. Revived in 2002, terminated by parliament in March 2012 and formally cancelled in October 2023, the project cost the country an estimated 2.2 to 2.5 billion dollars, including a 620 million euro arbitration award to the contractor, and generated no electricity.
lesson: Equipment ordered before the financing is secured becomes a liability that outlives the project and is still being paid for decades later.

title: The Alpine Wall
subtitle: Concrete poured at breakneck speed for a war that had already changed shape.
summary: Between 1939 and 1942 Fascist Italy poured 1.68 million cubic metres of concrete into a fortified line along its northern frontier, completing 306 bunkers in the South Tyrol sector alone and leaving 135 unfinished. Blitzkrieg had made static defence obsolete while the work was still under way, construction ceased in 1942, and the 1947 Paris Peace Treaty barred Italy from fortifying within 20 kilometres of the Austrian border.
lesson: A defence built to refight the last war is obsolete the day it is finished; confirm the threat model still holds before pouring the concrete.

title: The Nagymaros Dam
subtitle: A petition beat a treaty. The argument outlived both governments that signed it.
summary: Hungary and Czechoslovakia agreed in September 1977 to dam the Danube at Gabcikovo and Nagymaros, a scheme that would have inundated a 42-kilometre stretch of the Danube Bend north of Budapest. The Duna Kor campaign gathered over 140,000 signatures under communist rule, parliament halted construction on 12 May 1989, and the International Court of Justice judgment of 25 September 1997 found both states partly at fault without resolving the dispute.
lesson: A binding treaty cannot compel a later government to build what its own public has rejected; plan for the politics to change mid-construction.
locationRole: Planned dam site on the Danube Bend

title: The Charleroi Metro
subtitle: Four finished stations under a shrinking city, sealed for forty years.
summary: Belgium's 1960s programme gave post-industrial Charleroi a planned eight-line, 51-kilometre network with 69 stations, and by 1986 four stations at Neuville, Chet, Pensee and Centenaire were tunnelled, tiled and wired. Devolution shifted funding to a Walloon government that could not pay, the last Walloon colliery closed in 1984 and took the ridership with it, and the stations stood abandoned until EU stimulus funding paid for a scaled-down reopening due in 2026.
lesson: Infrastructure sized to a region's past employment will be stranded when the employment goes; size it to demand you can already see.

title: DART Underground
subtitle: Approved and cancelled in the same year. Now pencilled in for the 2040s.
summary: A 1972 study identified a 7.6-kilometre tunnel beneath central Dublin that would lift cross-city rail capacity from roughly 8,000 to 20,000 passengers an hour, and An Bord Pleanala granted the Railway Order in 2011 for a scheme costed at 3 to 4 billion euros. The government cancelled it that same year along with the whole Transport 21 programme, and by 2021 the National Transport Authority had shelved it until 2042 without a metre of tunnel being dug.
lesson: A permit is not a project; consent obtained without funding preserves the idea while the problem it was meant to solve keeps getting worse.

title: The National Hotel
subtitle: Seventeen storeys of Intourist glamour, stripped to the concrete and left there.
summary: Built between 1974 and 1978 on Chisinau's main boulevard as an Intourist flagship, the 17-storey National closed around 2004 after international tourism failed to recover from the 1992 Transnistria war. Privatised in 2006 and passed between owners, it was stripped by salvagers and then frozen by a court hold tied to money-laundering proceedings against its owner, and a 13-year-old girl died after falling from the building in November 2025.
lesson: An asset nobody can legally demolish or profitably restore is worse than a vacant lot; settle the title before the building becomes a hazard.
locationRole: Derelict hotel on the main boulevard

title: Ciudad Real Airport
subtitle: The relief airport for Madrid, and a footbridge to a station never built.
summary: Spain built a relief airport 200 kilometres south of Madrid, opening it in December 2008 at a cost above 1.1 billion euros on projections of 2.5 million passengers a year and a high-speed rail link that was never finished. It handled about 54,000 passengers in its first full year and roughly 190,000 in total before closing in April 2012, and the entire facility was auctioned in 2015 for 10,000 euros.
lesson: When the constraint your project exists to relieve is solved by someone else first, the business case is already gone; recheck it before you open.
locationRole: Terminal and runway in Castilla-La Mancha

title: The H-class battleships
subtitle: The dock outlived the fleet it was dug for, and is still working.
summary: Blohm and Voss laid the keel of Schlachtschiff H on 15 July 1939 under Plan Z, a six-ship programme whose later designs ballooned to 131,000 tonnes, and suspended work on 10 October 1939, six weeks after the war began. The ship was formally cancelled in November 1941 with roughly 3,500 tonnes of machined steel diverted to U-boat hulls and tank armour, while the Elbe 17 drydock built to hold it was completed in 1942 and remains in use today.
lesson: Long-lead capital assets assume a timetable; when the timetable breaks, the supporting infrastructure is often the only part worth keeping.

title: The Ellinikon Metropolitan Park
subtitle: A public park won the competition. Towers and a casino were built instead.
summary: After Athens moved its airport, a 2005 international competition drew over 300 entries and awarded a 530-hectare metropolitan park designed to draw about 80 percent of its water from the site itself. Legislation in February 2012 raised built-surface caps and permitted coastal construction, and Lamda Development's 2017 plan replaced the park with 6.2 million square metres of housing, towers up to 200 metres, a casino and just 65 hectares of green space.
lesson: Zoning rules, not design quality, decide what gets built; a scheme that depends on restrictive rules dies the moment the rules are rewritten.
locationRole: Former airport site on the Athens coast

title: The Thames Archway Driftway
subtitle: The riverbed won. The idea had to wait for a machine nobody had invented.
summary: The Thames Archway Company, incorporated by Act of Parliament in July 1805, drove a timber-lined pilot tunnel 1,027 feet under the river at Rotherhithe behind a 30-horsepower steam pump. Quicksand and repeated flooding defeated even Richard Trevithick and his Cornish miners, the company was dissolved in 1809, and none of the 49 alternative schemes put to Parliament was judged feasible until Brunel's tunnelling shield succeeded in 1843.
lesson: Some problems are not solved by more effort but by a missing invention; know which kind you have before spending the capital.

title: The London Pneumatic Despatch
subtitle: Capsules flew under the streets. Then they jammed, and nobody would pay.
summary: Formed in June 1859 with Thomas Brassey and W. H. Smith on the board, the company shot capsules through iron tubes beneath London at 30 to 40 miles an hour, opening its first line from Euston in February 1863 and eventually spanning about 1.5 miles. Capsules jammed repeatedly, loading took as long as ordinary street collection, the Post Office withdrew in 1874 and the company was liquidated in 1875 with the tubes left buried.
lesson: Peak speed is not throughput; measure the whole loading-to-delivery cycle before betting a business on the fast part in the middle.

title: Ivittuut
subtitle: The world's cryolite came from one fjord until a chemist made it cheaper.
summary: Mining at Ivittuut ran continuously from 1854 to 1987, producing roughly 3.7 million tonnes of ore and 2.15 million tonnes of cryolite, the flux that made aluminium smelting possible, with a wartime peak of 86,000 tonnes in 1942. Synthetic cryolite made from fluorspar undercut it from the 1960s and the accessible high-grade ore ran out, the mine closed in 1987, and the settlement was abandoned by about 2000 with some seven buildings still standing.
lesson: A natural monopoly on a mineral lasts only until someone synthesises it; treat resource rents as a countdown, not an annuity.

title: The Aérotrain
subtitle: It set its speed record and lost the country in the same year.
summary: Jean Bertin's hovertrain rode a cushion of air above a concrete guideway and reached 430.4 kilometres per hour on the Orleans test track on 4 March 1974, with government approval for an operational line following that July. The oil crisis, Bertin's death and the state's decision to back the conventional-rail TGV ended it, and the project was cancelled on 17 July 1977, leaving 18 kilometres of derelict monorail standing over farmland.
lesson: Being technically ahead does not beat an incumbent standard the state has already chosen to back.
locationRole: Test track across the Petite Beauce

title: Aramis
subtitle: Every cost cut removed the thing that made it different from a metro.
summary: Matra began work in 1970 on a personal rapid transit system whose small vehicles would couple into platoons and carry passengers point to point on demand. Cost pressure removed point-to-point routing in 1973 and mixed-use stations in 1977 and grew the vehicles from four seats to as many as twenty, platooning never coupled reliably on the Petite Ceinture test track installed in 1986, and the project was shut down in November 1987.
lesson: When each cut removes a defining feature, you are not descoping a product, you are converting it into a worse version of what it was meant to replace.
locationRole: Test track on the Petite Ceinture

title: Minitel
subtitle: France was online a decade early, on a network that could not become the internet.
summary: France Telecom launched Minitel in 1980 and rolled it out nationally in 1982, putting videotext terminals in homes for banking, reservations, directories and messaging and reaching roughly 9 million terminals and 25 million users by the mid-1990s. Its centralised, circuit-switched design and time-based billing could not be reconciled with a packet-switched open network, and the service was shut down on 30 June 2012.
lesson: A profitable closed platform resists the change that would save it, because the billing model and the architecture are the same decision.

title: Aéroport du Grand Ouest
subtitle: Half a century of planning, eleven years of occupation, no runway.
summary: First proposed in 1963 and granted a public utility declaration in February 2008 with a construction estimate of 580 million euros, the airport absorbed about 400 million euros in studies and legal procedure without a single earth mover arriving. Activists occupied the 1,650-hectare site from August 2007 and held it through repeated evictions, and Prime Minister Edouard Philippe abandoned the project on 17 January 2018 in favour of expanding the existing Nantes-Atlantique.
lesson: Decades of procedure are not progress; a project that cannot start accumulates cost and opposition at the same time.

title: Nokia MeeGo
subtitle: The reviewers loved the phone. The company had already chosen another platform.
summary: Nokia and Intel built MeeGo as an open Linux platform to succeed Symbian, and the N9 handset released in 2011 drew strong reviews and demonstrated the software worked. On 21 April 2011 Nokia announced a partnership making Microsoft Windows Phone its primary smartphone system, abandoning both platforms, and the replacement Lumia line lost 260 million euros in a single quarter in 2012 before Microsoft wrote off the entire handset acquisition in 2015.
lesson: Switching platforms buys speed only if the new one supplies the ecosystem you lacked; otherwise you have paid a transition cost for the same disadvantage.

title: Mongstad carbon capture
subtitle: Norway called it a moon landing. It ended as a test rig beside a refinery.
summary: Norway and Statoil agreed in 2006 to build the world's first full-scale industrial carbon capture and storage plant at Mongstad, targeting 2 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, and ministers compared the ambition to the Apollo landings. Cost projections reached about 20 billion kroner and the amine capture process demanded 25 to 30 percent additional energy, and on 20 September 2013 the full-scale phase was cancelled after roughly 7.4 billion kroner had been spent, leaving the test centre as the only result.
lesson: A pilot proves the chemistry, not the economics; an energy penalty that is tolerable at pilot scale becomes the entire business case at full scale.

title: The Zimenki radio observatory
subtitle: Nothing broke. The money stopped arriving, and the scavengers came.
summary: The Soviet Academy of Sciences established a radio astronomy station at Zimenki on the Volga between 1947 and 1949, and it ran for more than five decades on solar observation and radio astronomy research. Funding collapsed after 1991; at least one telescope was still monitored in 2002, all scientific work had ceased by 2010, and the RT-15-2 dish, control tower and scattered records were left to metal scavengers.
lesson: Research infrastructure fails through budget attrition rather than breakdown; the operating line, not the capital cost, decides whether it survives.

title: Olivetti's Elea mainframes
subtitle: Italy built a computer to face IBM. The bankers sold the division instead.
summary: Between 1955 and 1964 Olivetti developed the Elea series at Ivrea, with the Elea 9003 among the earliest computers sold internationally and a genuine claim to compete with American manufacturers. Low sales volumes, repeated financial instability and the death of lead engineer Mario Tchou in 1961 left the company exposed, and in 1964 its lenders required the entire electronics division to be sold to General Electric as a condition of continued operating loans.
lesson: Whoever holds your operating credit chooses which businesses you keep; a strategic bet survives only if it can be funded without them.
locationRole: Research and production works at Ivrea

title: The Interaction Design Institute Ivrea
subtitle: The school closed after five years. The circuit board its students made did not.
summary: Telecom Italia and Olivetti founded the institute in June 2000 on a five-year endowment, and it took its first students at Ivrea in 2001 under founding director Gillian Crampton Smith. The endowment was not renewed and the school merged into Domus Academy in Milan in 2007, but Wiring, built there by Hernando Barragan in 2003, and Arduino, built on it by five staff and students in 2005, became global open-source standards.
lesson: Fixed-term funding sets an institution's lifespan on day one; if the output is meant to outlast it, make the output independent of the institution.
locationRole: Campus in a former Olivetti research centre

title: Linnahall
subtitle: Tallinn's biggest room, shut after one safety inspection and never reopened.
summary: Built between 1975 and 1980 by Raine Karp and Riina Altmae for the Moscow Olympics sailing events, Linnahall gave Tallinn a 6,000-seat hall and an ice rink on the waterfront and served as the city's main venue for thirty years. Interior programming stopped after a safety inspection in April 2010, a 100 million euro redevelopment announced in 2017 has not happened, and the closed building costs about 883,000 euros a year to maintain.
lesson: A closed landmark still sends a bill every year; the choice is not between restoring and doing nothing, but between restoring and paying to decay.
locationRole: Seafront concert hall and ice rink

title: The Lasnamäe channel
subtitle: They blasted the corridor through bedrock and ran out of money for the trains.
summary: Soviet planners revived the sunken transport corridor from Eliel Saarinen's 1913 Grand Tallinn plan as the spine of Lasnamae, a district of eleven microdistricts eventually housing more than 115,000 people, about a quarter of the city. The 50-metre-wide limestone channel was blasted through bedrock and finished in 1995, but the excavation consumed the budget and no rapid transit was ever installed, leaving buses and trolleybuses running along the Laagna tee.
lesson: Building the corridor first commits the budget to the cheapest part to justify and the most expensive to dig; sequence the spending around the service, not the earthworks.
locationRole: Sunken transport corridor through the district

title: The Riga Metro
subtitle: Soviet planners called it transport. Riga read it as demography.
summary: From 1976 Soviet engineers designed a three-line, 40-kilometre metro with 33 stations for Riga, but high groundwater and sandy soils pushed estimated costs to 23 to 26 million rubles a kilometre, the highest of any Soviet system. A petition in Padomju Jaunatne drew 42,594 signatures against and 62 in favour, opposition fused with the independence movement over the roughly 30,000 Russian-speaking workers the build would import, and the project was cancelled in 1988 without a tunnel being started.
lesson: Infrastructure that changes who lives in a city will be judged as demography rather than transport; expect the argument to be fought on those terms.

title: The Daugavpils dam
subtitle: One newspaper essay stopped a dam and started a national movement.
summary: Construction of a 300 megawatt station on the Daugava began in 1979, with a reservoir that would have run some 65 kilometres and drowned the Daugava meanders. An essay by Dainis Ivans and Arturs Snips published on 17 October 1986 drew about 30,000 petition signatures, the Soviet Academy of Sciences judged the scheme unacceptable in 1987, and the Latvian Council of Ministers abandoned it on 5 November 1987 while the regime was still censoring the river's name.
lesson: Suppressing the name of a thing turns it into a symbol; censorship converts a technical objection into a political movement.

title: The Søringen lake motorway
subtitle: An elevated motorway across the lakes, stopped with its ramps already poured.
summary: Proposed in 1958 and argued for in Ole Noregard's 1965 technical report, the Soringen scheme would have driven a twelve-lane elevated motorway north to south through central Copenhagen and across the Soringen and Peblinge lakes. Demolition and the Bispeengbuen viaduct works began before local government reform in 1970, a strained city budget and public opposition turned the politics, and the scheme was cancelled around 1974 leaving the viaduct ending in mid-air.
lesson: Start the least reversible works last; visible half-built infrastructure is what turns an abstract objection into an organised one.

title: Roșia Montană
subtitle: Europe's largest unmined gold seam now sits under a World Heritage site.
summary: Gabriel Resources took the concession in 1999 for an open-pit project covering 23.88 square kilometres, with four pits and a 600-hectare cyanide tailings pond over 314 tonnes of gold and 1,500 tonnes of silver. Protests of 100,000 to 200,000 people in autumn 2013 led parliament to reject it, Romania designated the site as national heritage in December 2015 and UNESCO inscribed it in July 2021, and in March 2024 an ICSID tribunal dismissed the company's 4.4 billion dollar claim and ordered it to pay Romania's costs.
lesson: A licence is permission from one government, not from the public or from international law; either can withdraw it, and neither owes compensation for doing so.
locationRole: Mining concession in the Apuseni Mountains

title: NOHAB
subtitle: Sweden's locomotive works was paid in gold, then outlived by its own engines.
summary: Founded at Trollhattan in 1847 and building locomotives from 1865, NOHAB supplied 500 steam locomotives to the Soviet Union between 1921 and 1924 for 56 tonnes of gold and 230 million kronor, then diesels to Danish, Norwegian and Hungarian railways. European electrification and the oil crises destroyed diesel locomotive demand, the marine engine business went to Wartsila between 1978 and 1984, and NOHAB declared bankruptcy in 1979 and was liquidated by 1986.
lesson: A firm defined by one traction technology dies with it; diversification sold off for cash is diversification you no longer have.

title: Credit Suisse
subtitle: The scandals were survivable one at a time. The deposits left all at once.
summary: Founded in Zurich in 1856, Credit Suisse managed about 1.3 trillion Swiss francs and employed more than 50,000 people, but lost 5.5 billion francs to Archegos and over 3 billion to Greensill in 2021 and saw 111 billion francs of client money leave in the fourth quarter of 2022 alone. Swiss authorities forced a sale to UBS on 19 March 2023 backed by 100 billion francs of central bank liquidity, and the 167-year-old entity was dissolved on 31 May 2024.
lesson: Clients price repeated control failures long before regulators act; deposit flight, not a capital ratio, sets the deadline.

title: Builder.ai
subtitle: The code was real. The revenue was not.
summary: Founded in London in 2016, Builder.ai raised 445 million dollars from investors including Microsoft, SoftBank and the Qatar Investment Authority at a valuation above 1 billion, promising that its Natasha system generated roughly 80 percent of application code. Round-tripped invoices with VerSe Innovation inflated revenue by up to 300 percent, audited 2024 revenue came in near 55 million against a projected 220 million, and the company filed for Chapter 7 in late May 2025 after cutting about 1,000 staff in a single call.
lesson: Verify how revenue is recognised before you verify the valuation; circular invoices between friendly parties survive audit far longer than they should.

title: The Northwick Park trial
subtitle: Six healthy volunteers, one afternoon, and a rewritten rulebook worldwide.
summary: On 13 March 2006 a first-in-human trial of TeGenero's anti-CD28 antibody TGN1412 at Northwick Park Hospital dosed six healthy volunteers, all of whom developed cytokine storm and multi-organ failure within hours while the two placebo subjects were unaffected. The MHRA found no manufacturing defect and no protocol breach, only a compound that behaved differently in humans than in monkeys and mice; TeGenero filed for insolvency in July 2006 and regulators worldwide tightened first-in-human dosing rules for immunomodulators.
lesson: Preclinical safety is species-specific; where the mechanism itself differs between species, more animal testing does not reduce the risk.
locationRole: Clinical pharmacology unit at Northwick Park

title: Visaginas Nuclear Power Plant
subtitle: A town built for reactors voted against building any more.
summary: Lithuania authorised a replacement for the closing Ignalina plant by law in June 2007, planning about 3,400 megawatts of Western reactor capacity for an estimated 3 to 5 billion dollars. An advisory referendum on 14 October 2012 went 62.7 percent against, Latvia and Estonia withdrew their financing, General Electric Hitachi never advanced past a non-binding memorandum in July 2014, and the former energy minister who had championed it declared the project dead in April 2016.
lesson: A non-binding referendum still binds; once a project has been publicly rejected, no government can carry it through a decade of construction.
locationRole: Reactor site beside the Ignalina plant
